title: Embedding geometry: cosine, norms and semantic search
objectives: Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects embedding geometry: cosine, norms and semantic search with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. Use the vector calculator to compare cosine and raw dot rankings.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: An embedding is a learned dense vector whose geometry reflects a training objective. Related texts may be close, but distance is not a proof of equivalence or factual relevance. Query/document encoders may use different prefixes or projections; follow the model's retrieval contract.

Cosine similarity is dot(a,b)/(norm(a)*norm(b)). Unit-normalized vectors have cosine equal to dot product. Euclidean distance is a different ranking unless normalization and metric relationships are understood.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: For vectors [1,0] and [1,1], dot product is 1 and cosine is approximately .707. Normalize each vector by its own norm. Reject zero vectors or define their similarity explicitly; division by zero must not silently produce NaN scores.

Batch embeddings with stable document IDs, dimensions and model revision. Persist metadata about normalization, query/document prefixes and chunk version alongside the index. Changing any of these requires a compatibility check and often re-embedding.
sections.code:
import math
a=[1,0];b=[1,1]
cos=sum(x*y for x,y in zip(a,b))/(math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in a))*math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in b)))
print(cos)

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A new 768-dimensional embedding is queried against a 384-dimensional collection. Another index combines vectors from two model revisions with equal dimensions but incompatible geometry. Dimension checks catch only the first error.

Test identical vectors, orthogonal vectors, zero norms and revision mismatches. Evaluate retrieval on real relevant-document labels, including paraphrases, identifiers and multilingual cases if those are product requirements.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Use the vector calculator to compare cosine and raw dot rankings. The browser numbers are illustrative vectors, not outputs from a trained semantic encoder; the optional local sentence-transformer lab performs real text embedding.

Report Recall@K by query type and index revision. An SDET should retain hard lexical cases such as exact error codes because semantic similarity can confuse similar but operationally distinct failures.

mistake: A new 768-dimensional embedding is queried against a 384-dimensional collection. Another index combines vectors from two model revisions with equal dimensions but incompatible geometry. Dimension checks catch only the first error.
takeaway: Use the vector calculator to compare cosine and raw dot rankings.

title: Embedding compatibility, batching and multilingual evaluation
objectives: Embedding compatibility, batching and multilingual evaluation
Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects embedding compatibility, batching and multilingual evaluation with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. Release evidence compares retrieval Recall@K and latency by query slice before and after re-embedding.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: Equal vector dimensions do not imply compatible geometry. Two encoders can both produce 384 coordinates while mapping text into unrelated spaces. Mixing their document vectors or querying one index with the other encoder makes distance meaningless. Version the model revision, preprocessing, prefixes, pooling and normalization as one embedding contract.
Multilingual capability is a task requirement to test, not a property to infer from a model name. Error IDs and code snippets may also behave differently from natural-language paraphrases.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Batch text in a stable order with IDs, bound batch tokens and preserve per-item failures. Store a manifest beside each index generation. During an upgrade, build a new index, evaluate paired queries and switch atomically while retaining a compatible old generation for rollback.

For a query/document encoder, use the documented role prefixes. Evaluate exact codes, paraphrases, multilingual requests and ambiguous failure signatures. Check model revision and dimensions before issuing a query.

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A batch provider returns fewer vectors than inputs and the caller zips them silently, assigning later vectors to wrong IDs. An index upgrade changes normalization but keeps the old distance configuration. A cache reuses embeddings across preprocessing revisions.
Test cardinality, ID/order preservation, finite values, manifest equality and failed-item retry. Use separate cache keys for model and preprocessing contracts.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Release evidence compares retrieval Recall@K and latency by query slice before and after re-embedding. Report the cost of the full corpus migration and how long both indexes are retained.
SDETs should reject incompatible manifests deterministically before evaluating quality. A quality benchmark over mixed revisions cannot provide meaningful evidence about either encoder.

takeaway: Release evidence compares retrieval Recall@K and latency by query slice before and after re-embedding.
